questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: What a Gene Is and What It Encodes
questions.learningObjective: state what information in a gene specifies and what its product can be
questions.stem: A gene is a stretch of DNA, and students often assume its product must be a protein. Which description of what a gene encodes is correct?

options.text: A functional product, which is a protein for most genes but a functional RNA for others
A protein in every case, because DNA is a chemical script that is always translated
options.misconception: believes every gene is read by ribosomes into a chain of amino acids

options.text: A single amino acid, because each gene codes for one building block of the protein
options.misconception: believes one gene specifies one amino acid rather than a whole polypeptide

options.text: A protein only when the cell needs it, and an RNA only when the cell does not
options.misconception: believes the chemical class of the product is switched by the cell's needs

questions.explanation: A gene is a stretch of DNA whose information specifies a functional product, and that product is a polypeptide for most genes but a functional RNA for a substantial minority, including the transfer, ribosomal and regulatory RNAs that never reach a ribosome as a template. The distinguishing feature is the information carried, not the chemistry of the output, which is why a gene is better defined by what it specifies than by assuming it is a recipe. The tempting belief that DNA is always translated fails because many genes are transcribed and then used as RNA in their own right. The belief that a gene codes for one amino acid fails because the reading machinery takes a codon at a time but the unit of output is the whole chain. The belief that the product class follows the cell's needs fails because the product class is set by the gene itself and not switched on and off by demand.
questions.hint: Ask which products of gene expression are used as RNA rather than as a template for protein synthesis.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Genotype Set against Phenotype
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the allele pair an organism carries from the trait it displays
questions.stem: Two plants of the same species are crossed, and the offspring that display a recessive appearance are still distinguishable from the rest when bred. What separates an organism's genetic makeup from its observable trait?

options.text: The genotype is the pair of alleles carried, and the phenotype is the trait that genotype and environment together produce
The genotype is the trait that can be seen, and the phenotype is the allele pair hidden inside the cell
options.misconception: swaps the two terms, taking the observable trait to be the allele pair

options.text: The genotype is one allele from each parent, and the phenotype is whichever allele a parent supplied
options.misconception: believes the phenotype reports a parent's allele rather than the offspring's own pair

options.text: The genotype shifts when the environment shifts, and the phenotype is fixed at the moment of fertilisation
options.misconception: believes the allele pair is altered by the surroundings and the trait cannot be

questions.explanation: The genotype is the pair of alleles an organism carries, one from each parent, and it is fixed at fertilisation and inherited unchanged by its cells. The phenotype is the trait that is actually observed, and it results from the genotype read through the influence of the environment, which is why the two can come apart: a recessive-looking plant still carries an allele pair that breeding exposes, and two plants with the same allele pair can differ where the surroundings differ. The tempting belief that the terms are the same thing with different names fails because the gap between them is the whole content of genetic analysis. The belief that the phenotype reports a parent's allele fails because a parent's allele is only half the offspring's pair. The belief that the environment rewrites the genotype fails because an environmental effect changes what is expressed, not which alleles are present.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two terms would still be the same if the organism were moved to a different environment.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Why One Allele Can Mask Another
questions.learningObjective: explain dominance in terms of product amount rather than strength
questions.stem: A student claims that a dominant allele is a stronger allele and simply wins in a pair. Which mechanism actually accounts for one allele masking the other?

options.text: One copy of the dominant allele makes enough functional product for a normal trait, so the second copy is not needed
The dominant allele physically blocks the recessive allele from being copied or used at all
options.misconception: believes masking is a physical block on replication rather than on function

options.text: The dominant allele is copied more often, so it is present in larger amount in every cell
options.misconception: believes allele dosage reflects how often the two are replicated

options.text: The recessive allele is converted into a dominant form whenever a second copy is present
options.misconception: believes one allele is chemically altered by meeting its partner in the same cell

questions.explanation: Dominance is a statement about function, not about strength: a single copy of the dominant allele makes as much functional product as the cell needs, so the recessive copy contributes nothing that changes the outcome and the trait appears as though it were present in both copies. That is also why the label recessive does not mean weak, only that one copy is not sufficient, which is a property of the product rather than of the allele. The tempting belief that one allele physically blocks the other fails because both copies are present, both transcribed and both translated, and the recessive product is usually made normally. The belief that dosage reflects replication fails because both alleles sit at the same place in the same DNA and are copied with equal fidelity. The belief that the alleles are converted into one another fails because nothing rewrites one allele into its partner in a somatic cell.
questions.hint: Ask how many functional copies of the product a cell needs for the trait to appear normally.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Reading the Phenotype of a Heterozygote
questions.learningObjective: state what a heterozygote shows for a fully dominant allele pair and why
questions.stem: For an allele pair in which one allele is fully dominant, what does an individual carrying one copy of each show, and on what does that follow?

options.text: The dominant form, because a single copy of the dominant allele already supplies enough product
A blend between the two forms, because each allele supplies roughly half of the product
options.misconception: believes that two half-doses must add up to an intermediate trait

options.text: The recessive form, because the recessive allele is present and can be detected on its own
options.misconception: believes the presence of a recessive allele is enough for the trait to appear

options.text: Either form unpredictably, because the cell cannot tell which allele it holds
options.misconception: believes a cell randomly chooses one of the two alleles to express

questions.explanation: For a fully dominant allele the heterozygote shows the dominant form, and the reason is quantitative rather than a matter of the cell choosing: one allele produces enough functional product for a normal trait, so halving the dose to a single copy leaves the trait looking unchanged, and the recessive product that is also being made makes no difference to it. That is the sense in which the phenotype of a heterozygote is not an average of its two alleles, which is exactly what distinguishes this case from incomplete dominance. The tempting belief that two half-doses must produce an intermediate fails because the threshold for a normal trait sits below a single copy's output, not at the midpoint. The belief that a recessive allele is enough fails because one copy is by definition not sufficient. The belief that the cell picks one allele at random fails because both copies are present in every cell and are read together.
questions.hint: Ask whether the cell needs the product at all, or needs a particular amount of it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: What a Homozygous Condition Adds
questions.learningObjective: explain what homozygosity states about allele dosage and about risk
questions.stem: A clinician describes a person as homozygous for a condition rather than only as affected. What does that description add to what is already known?

options.text: Both copies carry the same allele, so a single copy of it is not enough to produce the trait
Both copies carry different alleles that together produce a milder form of the trait
options.misconception: believes homozygosity describes a mixed rather than an identical allele pair

options.text: Both copies lie on the same chromosome, so they were inherited together as a single unit
options.misconception: believes homozygosity is about physical position rather than allele identity

options.text: Both copies came from one parent, so no new allele was introduced into the family at all
options.misconception: believes two identical copies can only arise from a single parental source

questions.explanation: Homozygous states that both copies of the gene carry the same allele, and what that adds is the dosage statement that follows: one copy on its own is not enough for the trait, so both were needed. That is a different claim from saying a person is affected, which describes what is observed and leaves open whether one or two copies are involved, and the difference matters for prediction because a heterozygous parent passes the allele to half of the offspring while a homozygous parent passes it to all of them. The tempting belief that homozygosis describes a mixed pair fails because a mixed pair is by definition heterozygous. The belief that it is about position on a chromosome fails because the two copies of a gene always lie at the same locus, one on each homolog. The belief that two identical copies must come from one parent fails because a parental allele can be passed by either parent, so two carriers of the same allele readily produce a homozygote.
questions.hint: Ask what the word tells you about the number of copies needed for the trait to appear.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Codominance against Incomplete Dominance
questions.learningObjective: distinguish two heterozygote outcomes that are both called blending
questions.stem: In one system a heterozygote displays both parental gene products at once, and in another it displays a trait halfway between the two. What separates the two cases?

options.text: The first shows both products fully present, while the second shows an intermediate because neither allele dominates
The first shows an intermediate colour, while the second shows the two products separately on the surface
options.misconception: reverses which case gives a blended appearance and which gives two products

options.text: Both give a heterozygote two distinct appearances, but only the first needs one gene with three alleles
options.misconception: believes codominance depends on a three-allele system rather than on expression

options.text: Both give an intermediate shade, but only the second needs two separate genes acting on one trait
options.misconception: believes an intermediate phenotype must arise from two genes acting together

questions.explanation: The two cases differ in what happens to the two products. In codominance both are made and both are visible at once, so the heterozygote displays the two parental gene products simultaneously and the cell is not producing an intermediate. In incomplete dominance neither allele's product is dominant, so the single dose of each gives a trait that falls between the two homozygotes, and the intermediate is a genuine third phenotype rather than a mixture of two visible ones. The misleading feature of both is that a heterozygote looks different from both parents, which is why they are confused, but the mechanism behind the intermediate is a dosage effect and the mechanism behind codominance is simultaneous expression. The tempting belief that the two are reversed fails because it puts a blended colour where two products should be. The belief that codominance needs three alleles fails because two suffice. The belief that an intermediate needs two genes fails because one locus with two incompletely dominant alleles is enough.
questions.hint: Ask whether the heterozygote's cells are making one intermediate substance or two parental substances at once.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Reading a Sex-Linked Inheritance Pattern
questions.learningObjective: infer a sex-linked recessive pattern from which sex and which generations are affected
questions.stem: A condition appears far more often in males than in females, it seems to skip a generation, and affected sons are frequently born to mothers who show nothing. What pattern does that combination indicate?

options.text: Recessive and on the X chromosome, since a male's single copy of that chromosome is all he has
Dominant and on the X chromosome, since one copy would reach every child a father produces
options.misconception: believes a father passes his X to sons as well as to daughters

options.text: Recessive and autosomal, since a female carries two copies and can therefore hide the allele
options.misconception: believes an autosomal recessive condition must spare males because they hold two copies

options.text: Dominant and autosomal, since a single allele is enough for the trait to appear in either sex
options.misconception: believes a dominant condition would not favour one sex over the other

questions.explanation: The three observations fit a recessive allele on the X chromosome, and each one follows from the shape of that chromosome's inheritance. A male has one X and one Y, so a single recessive copy on his X has no second copy to mask it and the condition appears; a female has two X chromosomes, so one copy is normally enough to leave her unaffected, which is exactly how an allele passes unnoticed through a family and then appears in a grandson. The skipping of generations is therefore not a failure of the pattern but its usual behaviour. The tempting belief that X-linked dominant fits fails because a father passes his X to all of his daughters and to none of his sons, so such a condition travels through every daughter and not through any son, the reverse of what is described. The belief that it must be autosomal fails because a female's two copies do not protect her sons, who receive their single X from her. The belief that a dominant allele would favour neither sex fails because one X copy is a full dose for a dominant allele on that chromosome.
questions.hint: Ask how many copies of that chromosome a male has, and whether one is enough for the condition to show.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Why the Term Carrier Is Used
questions.learningObjective: explain what the word carrier records that the word unaffected does not
questions.stem: A person is called a carrier for a recessive allele even though the condition does not appear at all. Why use that word rather than simply recording the person as unaffected?

options.text: The allele is present and can be handed on, so the word records transmission rather than the absence of a condition
A carrier shows a mild form of the condition, so the word records a weak but visible trait
options.misconception: believes carrying an allele produces a partial expression of the trait

options.text: The person holds one affected copy and one normal copy, so the word records a mixed allele pair
options.misconception: believes carrier is a synonym for heterozygous rather than for hidden transmission

options.text: The allele stays quiet until something in the environment switches it on in the next generation
options.misconception: believes carrier status is an inactive state awaiting an external trigger

questions.explanation: The word carrier is chosen because the clinically important fact is not how the person looks but what the person can pass on: one copy of the allele is present, is not expressed because the second copy supplies enough product, and will be transmitted to about half the offspring. Recording the person only as unaffected would discard exactly that fact, which is the information a family needs in order to work out who should be offered testing. The term is a statement about transmission and dosage at the same time. The tempting belief that a carrier shows a partial form fails because with a fully recessive allele the phenotype is indistinguishable from anyone else's. The belief that carrier simply means heterozygous fails because it names the consequence, not the genotype, and heterozygous describes the pair rather than the risk to the offspring. The belief that an external trigger is waiting to activate it fails because the allele is being expressed normally and its product simply makes no difference on its own.
questions.hint: Ask what a clinician needs a family member to know before deciding who to test.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Reading a Single-Trait Cross of 500 Offspring
questions.learningObjective: infer the parental genotypes from a scored 3 to 1 phenotypic ratio

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Two plants of the same species are crossed. The 500 resulting plants are scored for one Mendelian trait that has two clearly separable forms. Three hundred and seventy-five of the offspring show the form that both parents display, and the remaining 125 show the alternative form, which neither parent displays. The scoring was done blind, by someone who did not know which treatment each plant came from.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what can be concluded about the cross that was made?

options.text: Both parents are heterozygous, and 3 in 4 carrying one dominant allele is the ratio that cross gives
Both parents are homozygous for the form they show, and the 125 are scoring or contamination errors
options.misconception: believes two true-breeding parents can produce an alternative form at all

options.text: One parent is heterozygous and the other homozygous, giving the 1 in 1 ratio such a pair produces
options.misconception: reads a 3 to 1 result as though it were the testcross ratio of 1 to 1

options.text: Both parents are homozygous dominant, and the 125 arise from a second gene acting by itself
options.misconception: invents an extra gene rather than accepting one locus at two alleles

questions.explanation: The alternative form appears among the offspring although neither parent shows it, so neither parent can be homozygous for it, and each parent must hold a hidden copy of it. Both are therefore heterozygous, and a cross of two heterozygotes gives one homozygous dominant, two heterozygous and one homozygous recessive in every four offspring, which puts three quarters in the dominant class and one quarter in the alternative class; three quarters of 500 is 375 and one quarter is 125, exactly the counts recorded. The tempting belief that two homozygous parents can produce a new form fails because a homozygous parent can only contribute the allele it holds. The belief that a 1 to 1 ratio applies fails because that ratio belongs to a testcross in which the partner's genotype is known to be homozygous recessive, and the 375 to 125 split is not 1 to 1. The belief that a second gene is needed fails because one locus with two alleles and both parents heterozygous already accounts for every class.
questions.hint: Ask which parental genotypes could still produce a form that neither parent displays.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Testing Independent Assortment on 320 Offspring
questions.learningObjective: check observed class sizes against the 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 prediction

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Two plants, each heterozygous at both of two independently scored traits, are crossed and the 320 offspring are scored for both traits at once. The four classes obtained are 180 plants showing both dominant forms, 60 showing the first dominant form with the second recessive form, 60 showing the first recessive form with the second dominant form, and 20 showing both recessive forms. The same four class sizes come out of a second, independent cross of the same two plants with 320 more offspring.

questions.stem: Which single statement accounts for all four class sizes in the note?

options.text: Two independently assorting heterozygous loci give 9:3:3:1, which is 180, 60, 60 and 20 out of 320
Each trait alone gives 3:1, so the joint classes should be 240 with the dominant form and 80 without
options.misconception: scored one trait at a time and forgot that both were being tallied together

options.text: The loci are fully linked, so all four classes are equally likely at 80 plants each
options.misconception: believes tight linkage produces equal classes rather than a parental-only pair

options.text: The ratio is 1:1:1:1, and the 20 double-recessive plants show a small error in scoring
options.misconception: takes a 4 to 4 to 4 to 8 result as the four independent products of a testcross

questions.explanation: A cross in which both parents are heterozygous at two loci that assort independently gives sixteen equally likely combinations, and those group into four classes holding 9, 3, 3 and 1 of them. Applied to 320 offspring those sixteenths are 180, 60, 60 and 20, which is precisely what the note records, so the independent assortment prediction is satisfied on both counts. The two smaller classes are exactly one sixteenth each, and their presence is the strongest single piece of evidence for assortment because a linked pair would produce almost none of the mixed classes. The tempting belief that scoring each trait separately explains the counts fails because it predicts only two classes, not four, and cannot produce the 20 at all. The belief that linkage gives equal classes fails because linkage preserves the parental combinations and creates the two mixed classes only rarely. The belief that the answer is 1 to 1 to 1 to 1 fails because that ratio belongs to a testcross and would put 80 in every class, including the double recessive one.
questions.hint: Write out sixteen equally likely combinations and count how many fall into each of the four scored classes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Letting a Pedigree Refute a Claim
questions.learningObjective: identify which statement a pedigree's transmission pattern rules out

stimulus.body: Field record (written for this course): A pedigree covers three generations of one family. The grandfather is affected and his wife is not, and one of their sons is affected. That son marries a woman who is not affected and has two affected sons and two daughters who are not affected. In a second branch the grandfather also had an affected daughter, and she has two sons who are not affected. The condition appears in every generation that has been drawn, and it never appears in a child born to two parents who are both unaffected.

questions.stem: Which single claim cannot be right, given both the record and how inheritance works?

options.text: That the allele is dominant and on the X, so every daughter of an affected father is affected
That a condition appearing only in sons must sit on a chromosome that a father passes to sons
options.misconception: believes a father hands his X to his sons as well as to his daughters

options.text: That appearing in every generation of one small family proves the condition is dominant
options.misconception: believes a short family history can settle dominance rather than suggest it

options.text: That a mother who shows nothing can never have a child who shows the condition
options.misconception: believes unaffected parents cannot produce an affected child, ignoring carriers

questions.explanation: A father gives his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y to every son, so a dominant allele on the X would appear in all of his daughters and in none of his sons. The record shows the opposite twice over: an affected father with two unaffected daughters, and an affected grandfather who had an affected daughter whose own two sons are both unaffected. That is not a discrepancy to be explained away but a direct contradiction of an unavoidable prediction, so the claim cannot stand. The other three claims fail on general grounds rather than on this particular record, and it is worth saying why they are still wrong: a father contribution to his sons goes through his Y and not his X, a condition can appear in every generation of a small family by chance when carriers marry in, and unaffected parents can certainly produce an affected child because a carrier is unaffected. The instructive point is that a pedigree can rule a pattern out far more readily than it can establish one, because a refutation follows from a demand the record plainly fails, while a confirmation needs many more families to be likely.
questions.hint: Ask what a father gives to a daughter and what he gives to a son, then compare that with the record.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Comparing Two Crosses for Linkage
questions.learningObjective: use recombinant class sizes to tell a linked pair from an unlinked one

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Two separate crosses are made, each between individuals heterozygous at a different pair of loci, and 200 offspring are scored in each. The first cross gives the four classes as 89, 11, 11 and 89, where the two large classes are the combinations the heterozygous parent already carried together. The second cross gives the four classes as 100, 0, 0 and 100, the two non-zero classes being the two parental combinations of that heterozygous parent.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which comparison best explains the difference between the two crosses?

options.text: The first pair of loci is linked, giving 11 per cent recombinants, while the second is unlinked, giving 50 per cent
The first pair of loci is far apart, giving 11 per cent recombinants, while the second is tightly linked at 50 per cent
options.misconception: believes a wide separation between genes gives few recombinants rather than many

options.text: Both pairs assort independently, so each should give 50 per cent recombinants and the 11 is a scoring error
options.misconception: assumes every locus pair behaves alike and dismisses one result as wrong

options.text: Both pairs are linked, but the first cross is larger so it detects 11 per cent and the second 50 per cent
options.misconception: believes sample size alone explains how many recombinants are found

questions.explanation: The first cross yields 22 recombinant offspring out of 200, which is 11 per cent, and a recombination frequency far below 50 per cent is the signature of loci that lie on the same chromosome and travel together. The second cross yields no recombinant classes at all beyond the two parental ones, so effectively every offspring received a parental combination and the recombinants are at the 50 per cent level that independent assortment or very wide separation produces. Note that a cross can show exactly zero recombinants in a sample of 200 simply because a rare event was not drawn, which is why the second result is described as effectively unlinked rather than as proof that recombination is impossible. The tempting belief that a wide separation gives few recombinants has the relationship backwards. The belief that all locus pairs behave alike fails because physical position differs between loci. The belief that sample size explains the difference fails because both crosses scored 200 offspring.
questions.hint: Add the two small classes in each cross and divide by 200.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Turning 200 Offspring into a Map Distance
questions.learningObjective: compute a recombination frequency and the map distance it estimates

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A cross between individuals heterozygous at two loci produced 200 offspring. The four classes obtained are 89, 11, 11 and 89 in the order of the four possible allele combinations. The two larger classes are the two combinations the heterozygous parent already carried on the same chromosome, and the two smaller classes are the two combinations that can only arise if a chromosome has been broken and rejoined between the two loci.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which single calculation gives the recombination frequency?

options.text: Twenty-two divided by two hundred is 11 per cent, placing the loci about 11 map units apart
One hundred and seventy-eight divided by two hundred is 89 per cent, giving a distance of 89 units
options.misconception: counts the parental classes as recombinants instead of the two smaller ones

options.text: Two hundred divided by twenty-two is about nine, giving a distance of about nine map units
options.misconception: inverts the fraction instead of dividing recombinants by the total

options.text: Eighty-nine divided by two hundred is 44.5 per cent, giving a distance of 44.5 map units
options.misconception: uses one parental class alone and so lands near the unlinked value

questions.explanation: Recombination frequency is the number of recombinant offspring divided by the total number scored, so the two smaller classes give 11 plus 11, which is 22, out of 200, and that is 11 per cent. For intervals short enough that a double crossover is rare, the same percentage read as a map distance is a good estimate, so 11 per cent corresponds to roughly 11 map units between the two loci. The calculation has to use the two recombinant classes and not the two parental ones, because the parental combinations are the ones that were present on the parent's chromosomes and are inherited intact whenever no exchange happens. The tempting belief that the 178 parental offspring are the recombinants fails because they are precisely the non-recombinant evidence. The inverted fraction fails because a frequency must lie between zero and one. The single parental class fails because using 89 rather than 178 nearly quadruples the result and lands close to the 50 per cent that would mean no linkage at all.
questions.hint: Count the offspring that needed a chromosome to be broken and rejoined, then divide by 200.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: What 212 Recombinants in 1,000 Offspring Allow
questions.learningObjective: interpret a measured recombination frequency as a limit on map distance

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A cross between individuals heterozygous at two loci produced 1,000 offspring. Two hundred and twelve of them show a new allele combination, and the two parental combinations account for the rest in equal parts of 394 each. Independent work has established that the two loci lie on the same chromosome. A further 2,000 offspring from the same cross produce 431 new combinations.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which statement about the two loci is best supported?

options.text: About 21 per cent recombination places them about 21 map units apart, and the second sample agrees
About 21 per cent recombination places them 21 units apart but on separate chromosomes
options.misconception: keeps the figure and rejects the note's statement that the loci are linked

options.text: Any measurable recombination rules out linkage, so the two loci must assort independently
options.misconception: believes linkage predicts no recombinants at all rather than fewer than half

options.text: The 788 parental offspring set the true distance at 79 map units, so recombination is the minor part
options.misconception: reads the parental percentage as the map distance instead of the recombinant one

questions.explanation: Two hundred and twelve recombinants out of 1,000 is 21.2 per cent, and because the note independently places both loci on one chromosome, that percentage is read as a distance of roughly 21 map units. The second sample of 2,000 giving 431 recombinants is 21.6 per cent, so the two samples agree to within the sampling error expected at these numbers, which is what makes the estimate worth acting on. The estimate is also a floor rather than an exact figure: a single exchange can restore the parental arrangement by chance, so at wider intervals the observed recombination frequency increasingly understates the true distance. The tempting belief that the figure settles where the loci sit fails because the note has already established the chromosome. The belief that any recombinants rule out linkage fails because linkage predicts fewer than half, not none. The belief that the parental percentage is the distance fails because 788 out of 1,000 is the complement of the same observation and carries the opposite meaning.
questions.hint: Divide the recombinant count by the total, then check the second sample gives a similar percentage.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Designing a Test That Establishes Dominance
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled cross that tests a dominance claim directly
questions.stem: A student claims that the allele for a tall plant dominates the allele for a short one, but has never tested the claim. Describe an experiment that would test it, and state the result the claim predicts.

answer.exemplar: Cross the proposed dominant plant with a true-breeding short plant, then score a large number of the offspring for height. Because the short parent can only supply the recessive allele, any tall offspring must have received the proposed dominant allele from the other parent, and if dominance holds every offspring should be tall; if the claim is wrong, the short parent would be masking a hidden tall allele and the offspring would segregate into tall and short. Running the same cross the other way round, with the short parent as the female or male parent in turn, tests whether the result depends on which parent supplies which allele, which is the way to catch a claim that rests on a parent-of-origin effect rather than on dominance. The things that must be held constant are the true-breeding status of the recessive parent, the growing conditions, the scoring procedure and the number of offspring scored. The prediction to record before starting is a single tall class with no short plants if the claim is right, and roughly equal tall and short classes if it is not, and writing that number down first is what stops the outcome from being reinterpreted afterwards.

questions.explanation: A dominance claim is tested by pairing the proposed dominant parent with one that can supply only the recessive allele, so that the offspring's phenotype cannot be attributed to anything else, and the reciprocal cross is needed as well to show the answer is not an artefact of which parent supplied which allele.
questions.hint: Ask what the recessive parent must be guaranteed to carry, and what the claim predicts for the offspring.

questions.topic: Genetics: Designing a Test for Linkage
questions.learningObjective: design a cross whose offspring counts distinguish linkage from independent assortment
questions.stem: A student claims two traits in a plant are inherited independently, having scored one generation of offspring. Design a test that would establish whether the two loci are linked, and give the result that would support the claim.

answer.exemplar: Make a cross in which one parent is heterozygous at both loci and carries the two alleles of interest on the same chromosome in a known arrangement, that is in the coupling or the repulsion phase, and score a large number of offspring for both traits together rather than one at a time. Counting the two non-parental trait combinations against the total gives the recombination frequency directly, and a frequency near 50 per cent supports the claim of independent assortment while a frequency well below it refutes it. A useful addition is a second cross using the same two plants with a different arrangement, because a frequency of 50 per cent is also what two very widely separated genes on one chromosome produce, and only the comparison of the two crosses shows whether the pair is far apart on one chromosome or on two. The constants that matter are the number of offspring scored, the growing conditions so that no environmental effect is scored as a genetic class, and the phase of the parental arrangement, which has to be known and stated rather than assumed. A sample of about two hundred offspring is enough to separate 11 per cent from 50 per cent comfortably, but a sample of twenty is not.

questions.explanation: The test has to score both traits in the same offspring, because linkage is a claim about the joint distribution of two alleles, and scoring them separately throws away exactly the information that distinguishes 11 per cent recombination from 50 per cent.
questions.hint: Ask what you would have to record in the same individual to see whether the two alleles travelled together.

questions.stem: Two plants are both heterozygous at a single locus with two alleles. First work out the fraction of their offspring expected to be homozygous recessive, then the number of such offspring expected among 1,024 seeds.

One half, which gives 512 of the 1,024 seeds
options.misconception: counts every offspring that received a recessive allele as homozygous

options.misconception: treats the cross as three heterozygous offspring out of eight rather than four

options.misconception: carries over a dihybrid fraction to a cross at a single locus

The belief that it is one sixteenth fails because one sixteenth is the double recessive fraction from two independent loci, not the recessive fraction from one, and a fraction borrowed from a dihybrid cross is the standard way this calculation goes wrong.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Genetics: Why a Pedigree Defeats Father-to-Daughter Transmission
questions.learningObjective: explain mechanistically why a pedigree rules out an X-linked dominant allele
questions.stem: In a pedigree an affected father has two unaffected daughters, and an affected grandfather had an affected daughter whose two sons are both unaffected. Explain why that pattern cannot be produced by a dominant allele on the X chromosome, and say what it does fit.

answer.exemplar: A father has one X and one Y, and a Y is the only chromosome he passes to his sons, so a son can never receive his father's X and therefore can never receive any allele that lies on it. Every daughter, by contrast, does receive his X in full, so a dominant allele anywhere on that X would appear in all of his daughters. The claim therefore makes an unavoidable prediction, that each affected father transmits the condition to every daughter and to no son, and the pedigree breaks both halves of it at once: the affected man in the second generation has two unaffected daughters, and the affected woman in the same generation has two unaffected sons, which is the second-generation man's X travelling on without effect because a single copy is not enough for a recessive allele. The pattern that does fit is a dominant allele on an autosome, which is transmitted to either sex with the same probability, and that is also what the rest of the pedigree shows, since the condition appears in every generation, never in a child of two unaffected parents, and always with at least one affected parent. The instructive point is that a pedigree is stronger at excluding patterns than at establishing them, because an exclusion follows from a demand the record plainly fails, while a confirmation needs many more families to be likely.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to rest on which chromosome a father passes to which child, because that single fact generates both halves of the prediction the record fails, and identifying the pattern that does fit requires checking the rest of the pedigree rather than stopping at the failure.
questions.hint: Ask which chromosome a father gives to a daughter and which he gives to a son.

questions.topic: Genetics: The Order of Work in a Mendelian Analysis
questions.learningObjective: order the stages that turn an observation into a stated inheritance pattern

Test the proposed genotypes with a cross in which the partner's genotype is known

The proposal is then put at risk by a cross in which the partner's genotype is known, which is the only way to separate the candidates that the first cross left indistinguishable. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: What Meiosis Reduces
questions.learningObjective: state what number meiosis halves and what it produces
questions.stem: A cell with 24 chromosomes divides to make gametes. What does meiosis reduce, and what does it produce?

options.text: It halves the chromosome number, giving four cells that each carry one set of 12
It halves the number of DNA molecules, giving two cells that each carry two sets of 12
options.misconception: believes meiosis makes two diploid cells rather than four haploid ones

options.text: It keeps the chromosome number, giving two cells that each carry one set of 12
options.misconception: believes meiosis conserves chromosome number the way mitosis does

options.text: It quarters the chromosome number, giving four cells that each carry one set of 6
options.misconception: believes the reduction is to a quarter of the diploid number rather than a half

questions.explanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number from two sets to one, so a cell with 24 chromosomes, which is 12 pairs, ends the division with 12 chromosomes in each of the four products. The halving is achieved by two divisions rather than one, and the reason it has to be two is that the homologues separate in the first division while the sister chromatids separate in the second, so both the chromosome count and the chromatid count have to be resolved. What is conserved, and this is the point of the two divisions, is that each gamete receives one chromosome from each pair, never both and never neither. The tempting belief that the products are diploid fails because two divisions followed by one set per product is the definition of the reduction. The belief that the number is unchanged fails because that is mitosis. The belief that it falls to a quarter fails because the second division separates chromatids of chromosomes already reduced to one set, so it does not reduce the count again.
questions.hint: Ask what a gamete needs for fertilisation to restore the original number.

Sister chromatids of one chromosome break and rejoin, at the stage when they separate

options.text: Whole homologues swap ends wholesale, at the stage when the cell is in division
options.misconception: believes the exchange moves whole chromosomes rather than short segments

Each event leaves two chromatids that are recombinant and two that are not, which is exactly what the class counts in a three-point cross record. The belief that it follows homologue separation fails because by then the homologues are in different cells. The belief that whole chromosomes trade ends fails because only short segments move, and the exchange is reciprocal rather than a wholesale swap.

Twelve chromosomes, six from each parent, mixed together before the gamete is made
options.misconception: believes a gamete contains material from both parents before fertilisation

options.misconception: believes a gamete carries both parental sets rather than one haploid set

options.text: Twelve chromosomes, all of them recombinant because every one has crossed over
options.misconception: believes every gamete chromosome is recombinant rather than only some chromatids

Within a single gamete, most of the 12 chromosomes are untouched by any exchange, and only the chromatids that took part in a crossing-over event are recombinant, so a gamete is usually a mixture of parental and recombinant chromosomes rather than entirely one or the other. The tempting belief that parental material is mixed before fertilisation fails because the gamete's chromosomes come from one meiosis only. The belief that a gamete is diploid fails because that is what makes fertilisation necessary. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: What Mitosis Conserves
questions.learningObjective: state what mitosis preserves and what it produces
questions.stem: A body cell with 24 chromosomes divides by mitosis. What does that division preserve, and what does it produce?

options.text: The chromosome number and the allele content, giving two cells that each carry 24
The chromosome number but not the alleles, giving two cells that each carry 24
options.misconception: believes mitosis reshuffles alleles among the two daughter cells

options.text: The chromosome number and the allele content, giving two cells that each carry 12
options.misconception: believes mitosis halves the chromosome number as meiosis does

options.text: Neither, because mitosis redistributes the chromosomes at random between the two cells
options.misconception: believes chromosome distribution in mitosis is random rather than exact

questions.explanation: Mitosis delivers an exact copy, so each daughter cell receives the same 24 chromosomes carrying the same alleles as the parent, and that fidelity is what makes growth, repair and the replacement of lost cells possible. The mechanism is what makes the fidelity credible: the two sister chromatids are separated so that one goes to each pole, and because they are copies made in the previous round, each pole receives a complete and matching set rather than a random selection. That is the difference from meiosis, where the homologues are separated in the first division and each product therefore receives a different half. The tempting belief that alleles get reshuffled fails because reshuffling is a feature of meiosis and of fertilisation, and a skin cell dividing does not change the individual's genome. The belief that the number halves fails because that describes meiosis. The belief that distribution is random fails because random segregation would produce aneuploid cells at a frequency nothing like the observed rate.
questions.hint: Ask how many cells leave the division and what happens to the sister chromatids.

questions.topic: Molecular Biology: The Three Stages of Translation
questions.learningObjective: name the three stages of translation and what each accomplishes
questions.stem: Translation is described as running in three stages rather than as one continuous step. Which division into stages is correct?

options.text: Initiation, elongation and termination, ending with the finished chain being released
Initiation, elongation and transcription, ending when the message has been copied
options.misconception: treats the final stage as the copying of the message rather than its reading

options.text: Activation, pairing and release, with no stage in which the chain is actually built
options.misconception: omits elongation, the stage in which the polypeptide is assembled

options.text: A single stage repeated for each codon, with no separate start and no separate end

Initiation is the assembly, in which the small ribosomal subunit binds the message, the initiator transfer RNA pairs with the start codon and the large subunit joins to give a complete ribosome positioned to begin. Elongation is the repetition, in which each matching transfer RNA enters, its amino acid is joined to the growing chain by a peptide bond and it leaves, while the ribosome advances three nucleotides. Termination is the ending, in which a stop codon is reached, no transfer RNA matches it, and a release factor frees the finished chain. The three-way split matters because the stages have different failure modes, which is why a message with no start codon, a message cut short and a message with a stop early give three different symptoms. The belief that elongation is missing fails because it is where the chain is built. The belief that there is no separate start or end fails because both are specific and separately regulated.

The counts are taken after the divisions have finished.

24 chromosomes in each of the four products, then 48 chromosomes in the fused cell

questions.topic: Molecular Biology: What a Testcross Establishes
questions.learningObjective: state what a testcross reveals that a single-locus cross cannot

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A tall plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a short plant that has been bred true for several generations and therefore contributes only the recessive allele. Two hundred seeds from the cross are grown and scored for height, and the result is 103 tall and 97 short. A second tall plant from the same population is crossed in the same way and gives 51 tall and 49 short.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what does the first cross establish that the parents' own appearance could not?

options.text: That the tall parent is heterozygous, because a hidden recessive allele appeared in about half the offspring
That the tall parent is homozygous, because tall offspring outnumber short ones by a small margin
options.misconception: reads a one to one split as a small majority and calls it homozygosity

options.text: That the recessive allele is dominant instead, because the short parent produced the short offspring
options.misconception: concludes the recessive allele is dominant merely because it was expressed

options.text: That the two traits are linked, because the two crosses gave slightly different tall fractions
options.misconception: treats ordinary sampling variation as though it reported linkage

Half the offspring being short, 97 out of 200, is what heterozygosity predicts, and the second cross giving 51 and 49 is the same result on a smaller sample. The belief that the recessive allele is dominant fails because dominance is defined by what a heterozygote looks like, not by which allele is expressed. The belief that linkage is involved fails because only one trait is being scored and the two tall fractions differ by sampling variation.

Each of the three positions of AAU is altered in turn to each of the four bases, giving nine single-base substitutions in all, and each resulting codon is looked up in that table: UAU, CAU, GAU, AUU, ACU, AGU, AAA, AAG and AAC.

Three are silent, five are missense, and one of the nine produces a stop codon

questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Designing a Test for Recombinant Gametes
questions.learningObjective: design a cross that reveals whether crossing over has occurred
questions.stem: A student claims that two alleles on the same chromosome never reach the same gamete because they travel together. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and say what result would refute it.

answer.exemplar: Score the offspring for both loci in the same individual rather than one locus at a time, using a cross in which the parent is heterozygous at both and carries the two alleles of interest in a known arrangement on one chromosome. If the fraction is well below a half, the alleles are travelling together as the claim says, and if offspring carrying the mixed combinations appear at a substantial rate, the claim is refuted and the pair is recombining. The number of offspring has to be large enough to separate the two possibilities, because a genuinely linked pair still produces a few recombinants, and a sample of twenty offspring cannot distinguish a rare event from a common one. The things held constant are the number scored, the growing conditions, the parent's phase, which must be known and stated, and the scoring rule, since a partly penetrant trait scored inconsistently would produce extra apparent recombinants that are really scoring errors. Confirming any recombinant offspring by a second, independent method is what separates a real recombinant from a mis-scored one, and it matters most for the small classes that carry the evidence.

questions.explanation: The test has to read both loci in the same offspring and score enough of them, because a crossing-over event is rare for tightly linked alleles and a small sample cannot separate a genuine low recombination frequency from no recombination at all.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Why One Message Can Be Read Many Times
questions.learningObjective: explain what sets how many times a messenger molecule is translated
questions.stem: A cell can make thousands of copies of one protein from a small number of messenger RNA molecules. Explain what allows this reuse, and name two things that limit how many times a given message can be read.

answer.exemplar: A messenger RNA molecule is not consumed by being translated: the ribosome reads it, builds the chain and leaves, and the message is still there to be read again, so a few molecules can serve as templates for a great many protein copies. That is the whole of the reuse, and it is why the number of protein molecules is set by the amount of translation rather than by the number of messages. The first limit is the message's own life, since every molecule has a half-life after which it is broken down and the supply of template falls, and a message with a short poly-adenine tail is degraded faster than one with a long tail, which is a large part of why the tail length is regulated. The second limit is whether the message is translated at all, because a message whose reading is blocked, whether by a small regulatory RNA, by a protein that blocks a factor, or by the cell having too little of a component, can sit unused however long it survives. A third limit worth naming is the number of ribosomes and of charged transfer RNAs available, since translation cannot run faster than the machinery allows, so a cell with plentiful messages and scarce ribosomes translates more slowly rather than making more. The instructive point is that control of protein output happens at several of these steps, which is why a cell can change the amount of a protein without changing how much of the message it has, and why two cells with identical amounts of a message can make different amounts of protein.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to establish that translation does not consume the message, and then tie the two limits to specific controls, one on how long the message lasts and one on whether it is read at all, rather than leaving them as general statements about degradation and regulation.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the messenger molecule after the ribosome has left it.

questions.learningObjective: state what a primer provides that a polymerase cannot supply for itself
questions.stem: Replication in a cell begins at a chosen place on the DNA, and copying there requires a short piece of RNA already in place. What does that short piece supply?

questions.topic: Molecular Biology: The Fixed Direction of a New Strand
questions.learningObjective: state the direction in which a polymerase builds and why it cannot reverse

The template is read from the end nearer the origin of replication rather than from the other end
options.misconception: believes a replication origin sets the direction the chain is built

options.text: The enzyme carries its active site at one end only, so it must travel along the template facing forwards
options.misconception: attaches the direction to the shape of the enzyme rather than to the chemistry

options.text: The nucleotides are released in a fixed order in the cell, so they can only be added one way round
options.misconception: believes the supply of free nucleotides constrains the direction

questions.learningObjective: classify described sequence changes by the mechanism involved

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Four changes are described in the sequence of one gene. In the first, one cytosine is replaced by a thymine, and the length of the sequence is unchanged. In the second, a stretch of four bases is deleted, and the length is four shorter. In the third, a single base is added, and the length is one longer. In the fourth, a run of two hundred bases is inserted elsewhere in the sequence, in a block that is a copy of a region found much further along the same sequence.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which single classification covers all four described changes?

options.text: One substitution and three sequence rearrangements that change length or copy a block
Four substitutions, because in every case exactly one base has been exchanged for another
options.misconception: counts all four as single-base changes regardless of their size

options.text: Two substitutions and two deletions, because an inserted block is treated as material removed
options.misconception: reads an insertion as a deletion and a substitution as two separate edits

options.text: Three frameshifts and one substitution, because any change of length shifts the reading frame
options.misconception: calls every length change a frameshift without checking the multiple of three

questions.explanation: Sorting the four by mechanism gives one substitution, a deletion, an insertion and a copied block, and the common feature of the last three is that they rearrange the sequence rather than alter a single position. A substitution exchanges one base for another and leaves the length untouched, which is the first description exactly. The other three change the length or duplicate material, and a block of two hundred bases copied from elsewhere is a rearrangement rather than a substitution because two hundred positions changed at once and the information is repeated. The tempting belief that all four are substitutions fails because only one base is exchanged in the first case. The belief that an insertion is a deletion fails because an insertion adds material and a deletion removes it, and the note distinguishes the two by the length changing in opposite directions. The belief that any length change is a frameshift fails because the reading frame only shifts when the change is not a multiple of three, and a four-base deletion and a two-hundred-base insertion are both multiples of one.
questions.hint: Ask how many positions changed in each case, and whether the length is the same.

questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Separating a Point Change From a Frameshift
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a single-base substitution from an indel by its effect on the reading frame

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A message of twenty-four bases is read as eight codons and its translation is recorded as methionine, alanine, phenylalanine, glycine, asparagine, a stop, alanine and proline, and the chain therefore has five residues. Two changes are then made in separate copies of the message. In the first, a single base in the second codon is exchanged for another. In the second, a single base is inserted immediately after the first codon.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which statement best separates the two outcomes?

options.text: The exchange changes one residue and keeps the stop, while the insertion moves the frame and loses the stop
The exchange changes one residue and moves the frame, while the insertion keeps the frame and loses the stop
options.misconception: believes a substitution shifts the frame and an insertion preserves it

options.text: Both changes move the frame, because any edit to a message is read as codons from that point on
options.misconception: believes every edit disrupts the reading of the message downstream

options.text: Both changes keep the frame, because the reading machinery re-reads the message in overlapping triples
options.misconception: believes the ribosome resynchronises after an insertion

The stop in this message sits at the sixth codon, and once the frame has moved the bases at that position no longer form a stop, so the chain is not ended there and grows past it in a new reading. The belief that the ribosome resynchronises fails because nothing tells it where the frame should restart.
questions.hint: Ask whether the length changed, and then whether the stop codon's three bases are still in frame.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: What Losing a Regulatory Region Does
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of removing a regulatory region on expression

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A gene is transcribed only in one of two tissues, and a short region lying well upstream of where transcription begins is required for that tissue's expression. A copy of the gene and its upstream region is carried into a cell line. When the upstream region is left intact, the reporter beside the gene gives a strong reading. When a 200-base portion of that upstream region is deleted, the reporter gives almost no reading even though the coding sequence beside it is unaltered and still reads correctly. Putting the deleted portion back in place restores the reading.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what does the deletion show about the upstream region?

options.text: It is a regulatory region needed for expression, since removing it silenced the gene without changing it
It is part of the coding sequence, since deleting it removed a stretch that the message needs
options.misconception: believes a silent upstream deletion must have removed coding material

options.text: It is a structural part of the gene, since the gene is no longer physically continuous without it
options.misconception: believes a regulatory region is needed to keep the gene in one piece

options.text: It has no function, since the coding sequence still reads correctly after the deletion
options.misconception: believes an unchanged reading means an unchanged function

questions.explanation: The deletion is a functional test of a region, and the design is what makes it convincing: the coding sequence is unaltered and still readable, so the only thing that changed is the presence of 200 upstream bases, and the only outcome is that transcription stopped. Restoring the deleted piece brings the reading back, which rules out any effect of the manipulation itself. That establishes the piece as regulatory, meaning it is required for expression rather than for the sequence to be transcribed into a protein, and it is the same kind of evidence that a knock-out gives for a coding region with the roles reversed. A regulatory region works by recruiting the proteins that assemble on a gene, so removing it leaves the gene intact but unrecognised, and a body cell with two copies of the gene can therefore make no protein at all. The tempting belief that the region is coding fails because the message is still read correctly and the loss is of transcription. The belief that a gene must be physically continuous fails because a gene includes its regulatory regions, and the coding sequence is only part of it. The belief that no function is involved fails because silence and readability are different properties.
questions.hint: Ask what stayed the same and what changed, since only one of the two can be explained by the deletion.

questions.topic: Molecular Biology: One Codon, Three Outcomes, Nine Replacements
questions.learningObjective: classify the nine single-base changes of a codon from the code table

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): One codon is read as GAG and the amino acid it specifies is glutamate. The code table is consulted for each single-base replacement of that codon, and the nine resulting codons are listed as GAA, GUU, GGC, GGU, GUA, UAG, AAG, AAG is repeated, and AGG. Two of the nine list entries are therefore the same codon, and the table gives the residue for each distinct one.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, how do the distinct replacements of this codon divide up?

options.text: One is silent, one gives a stop, and the remaining seven change the amino acid
One is silent, none gives a stop, and all eight change the amino acid
options.misconception: misses that UAG is a stop and treats a silent replacement as a missense one

options.text: Two are silent, one gives a stop, and the remaining six change the amino acid
options.misconception: counts a second silent replacement that the table does not give

options.text: None is silent, one gives a stop, and the remaining seven change the amino acid
options.misconception: overlooks GAA, which still names glutamate and is therefore silent

questions.explanation: Reading the table for the distinct codons settles it: GAA still specifies glutamate, so that one replacement is silent, and UAG specifies a stop, so exactly one replacement creates a stop codon and would cut the chain short at that point. The other seven name different amino acids and are missense. The note deliberately lists AAG twice, which is the detail that has to be noticed: a single-base replacement cannot produce the same codon twice, so the duplicate is a transcription slip in the list, and counting the nine entries as nine distinct codons would make the totals wrong. The eight distinct codons are GAA, GUU, GGC, GGU, GUA, UAG, AAG and AGG, and one silent, one stop and seven changed is eight in total. The pattern here is a property of this codon rather than a general rule, because whether a stop is one change away depends on where the codon sits, and a codon for tryptophan has no silent replacement at all because it is the only codon for that residue and has two that lead to a stop. The tempting three-way splits fail because each of them puts the silent, stop or missense count in the wrong place, and only the counts summing to eight distinct codons can be right.
questions.hint: Remove the repeated entry first, then look up each remaining codon in the table.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Why an Early Stop Destroys the Product
questions.learningObjective: explain why a message carrying an early stop is broken down

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A message is examined in a cell and a reading is made of how much of the protein it specifies is present. For the normal message, most of the protein is found. For a copy carrying a change that turns an early codon into a stop, almost none of the shortened protein is found, and the shortened message is found in a greater amount than the normal message. Introducing a second change that removes the newly created stop restores both the full-length protein and the normal amount of message.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what accounts for the three observations together?

options.text: The message with an early stop is read, made shorter, and then destroyed, so both protein and message shift
The message is never read, so no short protein is made and the extra message simply accumulates unused
options.misconception: believes the message is never read, so no short chain is made at all

options.text: The message is read, the short protein is made and is stable, so protein should be low only if it is degraded
options.misconception: assumes a shortened chain is automatically stable and so should still be present

options.text: The message is read normally, and only the last codon is affected, so the protein is full length
options.misconception: supposes the last codon alone is affected, so the chain would stay full length

questions.explanation: The three observations are what surveillance of a defective message looks like, and the mechanism produces all three together. A codon turned into an early stop means translation starts normally and stops early, so a shortened chain is made, which is the first observation and the reason the protein is not full length. The shortened chain is then recognised as the product of a message that ends nowhere, because the usual signal for a message worth keeping sits at the far end and is now missing, and the chain is destroyed rather than accumulated. The same reading of the message is a signal about the message itself, which is degraded instead of being used again, so it accumulates at a higher amount, which is the second observation. Putting the stop back restores everything, which ties both effects to that one codon rather than to the manipulation. The tempting belief that the message is never read fails because a short protein is made, so it was read. The belief that the short protein is stable fails because the stability is the thing that changes. The belief that only the last codon is affected fails because the change is early and everything after it is never reached.
questions.hint: Ask what the cell can tell about a message from where the chain it made stopped.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Testing Whether a Base Change Is Truly Silent
questions.learningObjective: design a test that distinguishes a silent change from one that alters the protein
questions.stem: A base change is reported as silent because it leaves the amino acid unchanged. Describe a test that would establish whether it is silent in every respect, and name one consequence it could still have.

answer.exemplar: Confirm the two things separately, because silent has two distinct claims in it. First read the sequence to confirm that the codon really has changed while the residue it names has not, which settles the first claim and rules out a sequencing error. Then measure the protein itself, in amount and by its mass and by its behaviour on a functional test, because a codon can change without the residue changing and still alter the protein, through a change in how quickly the message is read, in which transfer RNA the codon attracts, or in how the neighbouring residues pack, and a residue that is identical in name can differ in shape if a different one is used. The consequences worth naming are a change in the rate of translation, a subtle fold change from using a different transfer RNA, and a change in how the message is spliced if the codon sits at a splice boundary. A silent change is therefore not the same as a change that does nothing, and the practical significance of that is that a reported silent change is not a reason to stop looking. The constants that matter are that both versions of the gene are expressed in the same cell type under the same conditions, that the protein is measured rather than inferred from the sequence, and that a functional test is included, since a protein can have the right mass and still do its job less well.
answer.explanation: The design has to separate the claim that the residue is unchanged from the claim that nothing else changed, because a codon can change while the amino acid stays the same and still alter the message's behaviour, the protein's folding or the protein's function.

questions.explanation: The design has to separate the claim that the residue is unchanged from the claim that nothing else changed, because a codon can change while the amino acid stays the same and still alter the message behaviour, the protein folding or the protein function.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Finding Out What a Gene Is For
questions.learningObjective: design a comparison that attributes a lost function to one gene
questions.stem: A gene has no known function. Describe an experiment that would attribute a change in the organism to that gene rather than to the manipulation used to change it.

answer.exemplar: Remove the gene's function in one set of otherwise matched individuals and leave a matched set unaltered, then compare the two on whatever the organism does, and the second half of the design is putting a working copy of the gene back and asking whether the original change is undone. The first comparison is what attributes the effect to the gene, and the second is what shows the effect was caused by the loss of that gene rather than by some other damage the removal did along the way, which is the reason one manipulation is not enough. Running several independent removals and showing that each gives the same result rules out the possibility that one particular editing event happened to damage a neighbouring region, and a control in which an unrelated gene is removed in the same way shows the manipulation itself has no effect of its own. The constants that matter are the genetic background, which must be the same in both sets, the environment, which must be identical, and the scoring procedure, which must be applied without knowledge of which set a specimen came from. Reporting the effect as a measured change with its spread rather than as a description of one striking individual is what makes the conclusion one somebody else can test.

questions.explanation: The design needs a matched unaltered comparison, an independent-editing arm to rule out damage at the target site, and a rescue to show the effect follows the loss of that gene rather than the act of editing, because any one of those three alone leaves an alternative explanation open.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be shown before the effect can be attributed to the gene rather than to how it was changed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Testing Whether a Region Is Required for Expression
questions.learningObjective: design a comparison that isolates a regulatory region's contribution
questions.stem: A region upstream of a gene is claimed to be required for that gene to be expressed. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and name the outcome that would refute it.

answer.exemplar: Alter only the claimed region and read out expression with a reporter placed beside the gene, running the intact construct, the altered construct and an unrelated-region alteration of the same size in parallel in the same cell type under the same conditions. The third arm is the one that makes the test meaningful, because a construct with a different region of equal length deleted shows how much of any loss is simply the consequence of changing the construct, and a claim that is not more sensitive than that arm is not supported. Putting the deleted region back and recovering the reading is the confirmation, and moving it to a different position and still getting an effect distinguishes a region that has to be in one place from a sequence that carries information, which is a sharper claim than the original. If the reporter reading is unchanged after the region is removed, the claim is refuted, and the further finding that the gene still switches on and off at the right times in the right tissue would say the region is not required for expression at all, only perhaps for the level at which expression happens. The constants are the cell type, the amount of construct delivered, the time the reading is taken, and the size and position of the comparison alteration.

questions.explanation: The test has to alter the claimed region and nothing else, and the comparison arm of equal size elsewhere is what establishes that, because without it a loss of reporter reading cannot be separated from a general effect of rebuilding the construct.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be altered in the comparison construct so that a loss of reading means something.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Counting Primers on One Replication Fork
questions.learningObjective: count the primers needed on the two strands of a replication fork
questions.stem: One new strand at a replication fork is 10,000 nucleotides long and is made as fragments of 1,000, while the other new strand is the same length and is made in one piece. First work out how many primers the fragmented strand needs, then the total for that fork.

options.text: Ten primers on that strand and eleven at the fork, since the continuous strand needs only one
Ten primers on that strand and ten at the fork, since both strands start from a single primer
options.misconception: believes the continuous strand can begin with the same primer as the other

options.text: One primer on that strand and two at the fork, since one primer is used to make both new strands
options.misconception: believes a single primer serves as the start for both strands at once

options.text: Ten primers on that strand and twenty at the fork, since both new strands are made in fragments
options.misconception: believes the continuous strand is also made in fragments of the same size

questions.explanation: The fragmented strand needs one primer per fragment, because each fragment is a separate synthesis that has to be started from nothing, so 10,000 divided by 1,000 gives 10 fragments and 10 primers. The continuous strand is made from a single start and so needs one primer for its whole length, giving 10 plus 1, or 11 primers at that fork. The asymmetry is the point: the same fork that has produced 10,000 nucleotides on one side has used one primer, and 10,000 on the other has used ten, which is why the primer count on the fragmented side scales with the length being copied and the other does not. Every one of those primers is later removed and its place filled with DNA, which is a separate piece of work and is why the finished strands are both continuous even though only one was ever made in one piece. The tempting belief that both strands use one primer fails because the fragmented strand is started afresh ten times. The belief that one primer serves both fails because the two new strands are built against templates running in opposite directions and cannot be started from a common end. The belief that the continuous strand is also fragmented fails because it is not.
questions.hint: Divide the strand length by the fragment length, then add the one primer the other strand needs.

questions.stem: A message of 24 bases is read as eight codons, giving methionine, alanine, phenylalanine, glycine, asparagine, a stop, alanine and proline. First work out what a single base inserted just after the first codon produces, then what a three-base deletion of the asparagine codon produces.

options.text: An eight-residue chain with no stop, and a four-residue chain that keeps its stop
A four-residue chain that keeps its stop, and an eight-residue chain with no stop
options.misconception: swaps which edit destroys the stop and which preserves it

options.text: A five-residue chain with no stop, and a four-residue chain that keeps its stop
options.misconception: believes a one-base insertion shortens the chain rather than moving the frame

options.text: An eight-residue chain with no stop, and a five-residue chain that keeps its stop
options.misconception: believes removing a whole codon leaves the chain as long as it was
