questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Reading Redundancy as a Filter on Change
questions.learningObjective: explain what redundancy implies about which base changes are tolerated
questions.stem: Most amino acids are named by more than one codon, two are named by only one, and three are named by none as a sense codon. Explain what this distribution does and does not allow a base change to do.

answer.exemplar: Redundancy is a statement about which positions in a message can be altered without the protein changing, and the shape of the table shows that the answer is far from uniform. The code has 64 codons of which 61 name an amino acid and 3 signal termination, so twenty residues share 61 codons; most are named by two, four residues by four, three by six, and tryptophan and methionine by one each. A change to a codon that has a synonym therefore leaves the residue unaltered, which is a silent change, and a change to a codon with no synonym is always visible in the protein. The unevenness is the informative part. A codon for methionine or tryptophan can be altered in no way that keeps the same residue, so a change there is always missense or, for tryptophan, often nonsense, since two single-base changes from it reach a stop. That asymmetry is the reason a protein's sequence carries more information about its function than a random sequence of the same composition would, and the reason a coding region is under stronger constraint than the parts of a message that are not translated. What redundancy does not do is repair anything, detect anything, or widen the range of residues a codon can reach. It is not a backup copy and nothing compares two codons as a check. It also does not mean a change is harmless, because a codon can change while the residue stays the same and still alter how fast the message is read, which transfer RNA the codon attracts, and which of the two is used matters to how efficiently translation proceeds and, through that, to how much protein is made.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to draw the distinction between which changes leave the protein identical and which leave the cell's behaviour identical, because the two come apart and the second is the one that matters when a change is called silent.
questions.hint: Ask how many codons name the rare residues, and what that implies for a change at one of them.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Why No Transfer RNA Matches a Stop Codon
questions.learningObjective: explain why termination is a signal rather than an absence
questions.stem: A stop codon occupies a site in the ribosome and translation ends, yet no transfer RNA ever matches one. Explain how an ending can be produced by the absence of anything, and what would be different if a transfer RNA did match.

answer.exemplar: The ending is produced by a positive signal rather than by the absence of one, and the mechanism is that a separate protein occupies the site instead. Three codons are read as termination, and each has no transfer RNA whose anticodon pairs with it, which is the same structural fact that guarantees a mistake here cannot be made by a transfer RNA carrying an amino acid. What arrives instead is a release factor, a protein whose shape fits the site the way an anticodon would, and whose presence triggers the hydrolysis of the bond that holds the finished chain to the last transfer RNA. The chain is released, the ribosome comes apart, and both are reused. So the absence of a matching transfer RNA is not what ends translation; it is what allows a different molecule to act, and that distinction matters practically, because a system that ended translation merely by having no matching transfer RNA would have no way to distinguish a real end from a message that had lost a transfer RNA by accident. If a transfer RNA did match a stop codon, the chain would be extended by an extra residue at every stop position, translation would never finish, and the message would have to be dismantled by a separate mechanism while the ribosome kept going. That is the practical meaning of a stop codon being a codon rather than a gap: it is a readable instruction that switches the ribosome from one set of partners to another, and it is why introducing one early is a change with a predictable effect, namely a shorter product that is usually destroyed because the message it came from ends nowhere.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to show that termination is actuated rather than merely permitted, because the absence of a matching transfer RNA is the condition that lets a release factor act rather than the cause of the ending, and that is what makes a stop codon a readable instruction.
questions.hint: Ask what occupies the site when no transfer RNA matches, and what that molecule does.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Molecular Biology: Ordering the Events of a Translation
questions.learningObjective: order the events of initiation, elongation and termination
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order they occur as a protein is built on a message.

options.text: The small subunit binds the message and the initiator transfer RNA pairs with the start codon
The large subunit joins, completing a ribosome positioned at the start of the message
Each matching transfer RNA enters, delivers its amino acid and leaves as the ribosome advances
The ribosome reaches a codon that no transfer RNA matches as the chain nears its end
A release factor frees the finished chain and the ribosome comes apart for reuse

questions.explanation: Initiation comes first because nothing can happen until the ribosome is bound to the message and positioned: the small subunit attaches and the initiator transfer RNA pairs with the start codon, and only then is the position fixed, because a ribosome that assembled in the wrong place would build a protein from the wrong beginning. The large subunit then joins, which completes a functional ribosome and commits it to the frame, and from that point elongation is the same repeated cycle over and over, each transfer RNA entering, delivering its amino acid and leaving as the ribosome moves three bases. Termination is reached not because a signal arrives but because the reading runs off the end of the message's codons, and the release factor then frees the chain and the ribosome disassembles. The order is forced by dependency rather than by convention: no amino acid can be delivered before the ribosome exists, the frame cannot be fixed before the initiator is placed, and nothing can be released before there is a chain. The wrong order that elongates before the large subunit joins fails because a partial ribosome cannot perform the transfer at all. The wrong order that releases before elongation fails because there is no chain to release.
questions.hint: Ask which event fixes where reading will begin, since everything after it depends on that.

questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a free amino acid becomes part of a protein
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order by which a free amino acid in the cell becomes part of a finished protein.

The amino acid is activated and joined to that transfer RNA at its acceptor end
The charged transfer RNA reaches the ribosome and pairs with the matching codon
The amino acid is transferred to the end of the growing chain as a peptide bond forms
